questions: What does a dozen count, and what does a mole count?
Why do chemists weigh moles instead of counting particles?
segments.say: A mole is a counting word. Watch the dozen eggs first: a dozen counts 12. Then watch the particles: a mole counts 6.02 × 10²³ particles - far too many to count one by one, so chemists weigh moles instead of counting them. Tell your partner: what is the same about a dozen and a mole, and what is different?

questions: What is the molar mass of carbon-12?
What does n = m / M give for 12 g of carbon?
segments.say: Mass to moles. The mass of one mole of carbon-12 is 12 g - that is its molar mass. Follow the carbon onto the balance, watch the reading reach 12 g, and work it with me: n = m / M = 12 / 12 = 1 mol. The scale counted the atoms for you.

questions: What is the mole ratio in 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O?
How much oxygen is needed for 4 mol of hydrogen?
segments.say: Mole ratios. Balanced equations count moles, not grams: two moles of hydrogen react with one of oxygen to make two of water, a ratio of 2 : 1 : 2. Watch the scale-up: double the hydrogen and you must double the oxygen - the ratio never changes.

questions: Do one mole of carbon and one mole of water weigh the same?
What decides the mass of one mole?
segments.say: A common mistake: one mole of everything weighs the same. Watch the two pans: one mole of carbon reads 12 g and one mole of water reads 18 g. Same number of particles, different mass - the molar mass decides. Say it with me: mass = moles x molar mass.

questions: How do you turn a mass into moles?
What would you say to someone who thinks every mole weighs the same?
segments.say: Here is the trap, sprung on purpose: it is tempting to think every mole weighs the same, because a mole feels like one fixed bag. Watch the scenes again: the count is fixed, the mass is not. Now work through the worksheet in pairs, checking each answer against the trap section of your student notes. Last, the exit ticket - on your own, no talking - and remember: if you can turn mass into moles and name the molar mass, you have cracked today's lesson.
segments.watchFor: One mole of anything weighs the same. Listen for students who say exactly this when they compare moles of different substances. Send them back to the formula: Mass = moles x molar mass: one mole of hydrogen is 1 g but one mole of oxygen is 16 g.
